narrative:
The model determined that you have a 76.6% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this predicted risk is quite high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class ranking after the third year of law school was the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction heavily toward failure. Being in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) is substantially lower than the average ranking of about 5.8 among students who were accepted, signaling that your later academic performance was a major concern.

Your first-year class ranking was the second most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure. Placing in the second decile is well below the average of 6.0 for accepted students, reinforcing the pattern of academic struggle.

Your LSAT score was the third most influential factor, but it worked in the opposite direction. The score of 29.5 pulled the prediction slightly toward passing. However, this positive effect was not nearly strong enough to overcome the academic ranking concerns.

Your undergraduate GPA of 2.4 (versus an average of 3.23 among accepted students), upper-middle family income, and plan to attend full-time played smaller roles and did not change the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record if you retake courses, consider retaking the LSAT to raise that score significantly, or explore schools and programs with different admissions criteria that weigh other strengths more heavily.
